<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but B sustained a more damaging institutional-realism attack across rounds. B's twin pillars—enforcement capture falling on smallholders and leakage to weaker-oversight regions—were never fully neutralized by A. A's proposed fix (condition new permits on boundary compliance, suspend for unauthorized clearing) still required the same disputed-boundary adjudication and legal-outlasting capacity B identified as absent, and B explicitly showed this in Rebuttal 2 ("PRO hasn't built that capacity by describing it; PRO has just renamed the problem 'permitting'"). B also successfully weaponized A's own hedge that leakage "must count against us" and can't be sized, turning it into a concession that the benefit side of PRO's ledger is unproven—a framing A's closing merely reasserted rather than rebutted. A landed a genuine hit by pointing out B's own alternative ("enforce existing maps") relies on the same weak state capacity B uses to indict A's proposal, but B's rejoinder (marginal effort vs. wider surface area) was a plausible, if not fully proven, distinction that blunted the tu quoque. A's moral core—externalities imposed on non-consenting neighbors, irreversibility of peat/forest loss—remained strong but under-defended against the "does the remedy actually work" critique. B's closing crystallized the clash more effectively with the "who bears the risk of being wrong" framing, giving a cleaner decision rule than A's restatement of symmetric costs.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 exchange (B4.3-B4.4), where B turns A's own admission that leakage "must count against us" and cannot be sized into a concession that PRO's benefit case is unproven, while showing A's permitting mechanism still requires the exact adjudicative capacity CON identified as absent—decisively pressuring A's central mechanism and burden framing for the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
